Issues.Title: Use a build-owned static asset for browser tools activation
Issues.Body:
## Summary

Replace the provider-owned `GET /_framework/dotnet-browser-tools/hot-reload-settings.json` activation response with an application-hosted, build-only Static Web Asset at the same stable route. A normal build writes `{ "hotReload": false }` in `obj/<configuration>/<tfm>/dotnet-watch/`; Watch changes that file to `true` after compilation before launch/relaunch, restores `true` after in-process rebuilds, and resets it on graceful shutdown. Writes are skipped when bytes are unchanged. No user source files are modified.

The settings asset is non-fingerprinted, excluded from compression and publish, and carries `Cache-Control: no-store` endpoint metadata. Its endpoint order (`-1001`) precedes existing host fallback endpoints. The Web and WebAssembly initializers use `fetch(..., { cache: 'no-store' })` with a distinct UUID-based `If-None-Match` validator on each settings request. The Gateway proxy now forwards only `/connect` and `/clear-cache`; the hosting startup and provider no longer forward/serve settings. The build-owned JavaScript, RSA public/private key split, application-hosted trusted code, authenticated WebSocket/replay, and MVC/Blazor activation paths remain unchanged.

**Compared with the merged endpoint approach (#56118 and #56234):** provider availability no longer controls activation through a forwarded HTTP response. The build owns the disabled settings document and Watch toggles that one output file; executable browser tools and the public key still come exclusively from the application, while the provider remains limited to the authenticated socket and cache-clear routes. This PR targets **main**, not either prior PR branch.

## Incrementality and fast up-to-date check

Normal builds update a private, non-asset completion marker *after* restoring the settings file to false. Design-time builds expose `UpToDateCheckBuilt` with that marker as the output and the settings file as `Original`, following the [project-system fast up-to-date-check contract](https://github.com/dotnet/project-system/blob/main/docs/up-to-date-check.md#transformed-files). A later watch write makes settings newer than the marker, so Visual Studio schedules an ordinary build rather than skipping MSBuild. That build restores false and advances the marker; repeated ordinary builds leave settings and generated metadata unchanged. The marker is removed on Clean and is neither a Static Web Asset nor published. Hosted WebAssembly reports the pair for the browser-facing client, not the server.

The SDK tests follow the repository's design-time build pattern with `DesignTimeBuild=true` and `BuildingInsideVisualStudio=true`, and emulate the [project-system test cases](https://github.com/dotnet/project-system/blob/main/tests/Microsoft.VisualStudio.ProjectSystem.Managed.VS.UnitTests/ProjectSystem/VS/UpToDate/BuildUpToDateCheckTests.cs) for source-newer, source missing, and destination missing. They read the real generated `UpToDateCheckBuilt`/`Original` pair, apply the corresponding existence/timestamp decision, and call the SDK build only when needed. The Web/Gateway scenarios verify skip → build → skip, and missing settings/marker cases verify the pair stays available and the next build recreates the missing file. These tests do not run or depend on the Visual Studio CPS check itself.

## Validation

- `build.cmd -nobl /v:q`: passed (0 warnings, 0 errors).
- Focused Visual Studio-style FUTDC simulation and hosted-client ownership: 5/5; prior browser-tools SWA integration: 22/22, including build → settings change → build reset, unchanged repeated build, Web/Gateway design-time item collection, hosted-client ownership, publish exclusion and Clean removal. 34 affected SWA baseline tests: 34/34; standalone and hosted WASM baseline tests: 3/3; hosting-startup tests: 5/5; watch routing and settings tests: 15/15; real Watch graceful-shutdown/settings tests: 14/14. Updated affected checked-in build baselines.
- The reset test asserts the original disabled bytes return after a watch-style file change; `LastWriteTimeUtc` advances only for the changed settings file; the build manifest reflects its current timestamp at SWA's one-second precision; and a subsequent unchanged build preserves the settings bytes, timestamp, configuration timestamp, and manifest bytes. The design-time tests assert the settings `Original`/marker `UpToDateCheckBuilt` pair and that a changed settings file becomes newer than the marker before a build, but not afterward.
- Running server-hosted Web and standalone Blazor Gateway tests: fresh `If-None-Match: "browser-tools-<UUID>"` requests returned HTTP 200 with false → true → true → false → false from the *same host*, including changes to the obj file after compilation without rebuilding/restarting the host. Build endpoints are single-route, non-fingerprinted, uncompressed, no-store metadata, and publish/clean exclude/remove the asset.
- Actual browser evaluation of the generated Web initializer observed five 200 responses, five distinct UUID validators, false → true → true → false → false, `cache: 'no-store'`, unchanged app PID **30428**. The generated WASM initializer on the Gateway observed four 200 responses and four distinct UUID validators across false → true → true → false; its runtime activation flag followed true/false. No application restart was needed.

## Cross-repository follow-up

Removing the existing Gateway and Razor Components fallback endpoints requires a separate dotnet/aspnetcore PR; none are changed here. The SWA settings endpoint takes precedence while those fallbacks remain.

Issues.Title: Dotnetup: Proposal for improving uninstall and list
Issues.Body:
The relationship between an install spec and an installed version can be a source of confusion when using dotnetup.  Some of the main places this can happen are:

- You might ask it to uninstall a specific version that is installed, and it gives you an error that there's no install spec matching that channel
- You might ask it to uninstall a version or channel, and it successfully removes the spec but doesn't remove any installation, because it's referenced by other specs
- You can see that an SDK is installed, but can’t tell what is keeping it installed.  Separate lists of specs and installations don’t show which channel or repository references the version you want to remove

This proposal aims to improve this by improving the behavior of the uninstall commands and the output of `dotnetup list`.

It is an attempt to address the problems raised in https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/issues/56228, but this proposal attempt to address them a bit differently (by sticking with the install and uninstall verbs and improving the behavior and output to help users better understand).

Issues.Title: Externalize localized resources from the NativeAOT CLI
Issues.Body:
## Summary

This change reduces the size of `dotnet-aot` by loading localized CLI strings from the managed satellite assemblies already present in the SDK layout instead of embedding duplicate satellite payloads into the NativeAOT image.

It adds:

- a shared string-resource runtime in `Microsoft.DotNet.Cli.CoreUtils`;
- an analyzer-only RESX generator for cached CLI resource accessors;
- PE-backed neutral and satellite resource readers that do not load or execute the managed assemblies;
- three private NativeAOT resource modes:
  - `Embedded`
  - `ExternalLocalized` — the new default
  - `ExternalAll` — measurement-only
- strict neutral-resource preflight before the NativeAOT commit point;
- tolerant exact → parent → neutral fallback for localized satellites; and
- mode-aware NativeAOT tests, layouts, and performance tooling.

The resource reader and generator were adapted from the prototype in `JeremyKuhne/touki`. Only the required string-resource closure was brought into the SDK, using SDK namespaces and license headers. This adds no runtime package dependency or new runtime assembly.

## Change size

The upstream diff contains 108 files, 12,151 added lines, and 69 deleted lines:

| Area | Files | Added | Deleted | Share of added lines |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Product code and project wiring | 75 | 9,165 | 51 | 75.4% |
| Tests and test selection | 26 | 2,499 | 11 | 20.6% |
| Reusable validation/performance tooling | 1 | 384 | 0 | 3.2% |
| Documentation and contributor guidance | 6 | 103 | 7 | 0.8% |

The product portion breaks down as:

| Product area | Added | Deleted |
|---|---:|---:|
| CoreUtils resource runtime | 5,961 | 0 |
| Analyzer-only resource generator | 2,541 | 0 |
| NativeAOT provider and resource modes | 562 | 38 |
| Managed-owner and project wiring | 101 | 13 |

The adapted low-level runtime and generator account for 8,502 lines, or 92.8% of the product additions. The NativeAOT behavior change itself is approximately 600 lines, with another approximately 100 lines of managed/project integration.

## Motivation

The final SDK already contains the managed CLI owner assemblies and their localized satellite assemblies. NativeAOT was also receiving satellite inputs through `@(IlcSatelliteAssembly)`, causing the same localized payloads to be embedded into `dotnet-aot.dll`.

Reusing the existing SDK-layout files removes that duplication while preserving the managed CLI's resource names, generated properties, culture fallback, and localized output.

## Design

### Shared resource runtime

The runtime implementation lives in `Microsoft.DotNet.Cli.CoreUtils` under:

```text
Microsoft.DotNet.Cli.Resources
Microsoft.DotNet.Cli.Resources.Internal
```

It supports:

- indexed string lookup from embedded `.resources`;
- neutral resources read from managed owner assemblies as PE data;
- localized resources read from managed satellite assemblies as PE data;
- assembly name, culture, version, and public-key-token validation;
- exact, parent, and neutral fallback;
- concurrency-safe table and culture caching; and
- strict or fallback-on-localized-failure probing.

External assemblies are parsed as trusted deployment data. They are never loaded or executed, and serialized user values are never activated.

The resource runtime is compiled only for `$(SdkTargetFramework)`, leaving the net472 CoreUtils build unchanged.

### Generated accessors

`Microsoft.DotNet.Cli.Resources.Generator` is a new analyzer-only `netstandard2.0` project.

It emits strongly typed accessors with:

- one cached field per resource property;
- constant-time cache replacement on culture changes;
- a process-wide manager provider selected before first access; and
- no runtime dependency on the generator assembly.

The managed CLI uses normal runtime-satellite behavior when no provider is registered.

### NativeAOT provider lifecycle

`NativeEntryPoint` now:

1. applies the UI-language override;
2. resolves the versioned SDK directory;
3. configures or preflights the selected resource mode;
4. falls back to the managed CLI immediately if `ExternalAll` preflight fails;
5. only then initializes telemetry, first-run behavior, and parsing.

This keeps neutral-resource failure before the NativeAOT commit point and avoids replaying an invocation after output or mutation.

### Resource modes

| Mode | Neutral strings | Localized strings | Intended use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Embedded` | Native image | Existing embedded inputs plus managed satellites for referenced SDK owners | Baseline |
| `ExternalLocalized` | Native image | Existing managed SDK satellites | Default |
| `ExternalAll` | Existing managed owner assemblies | Existing managed SDK satellites | Measurement only |

In both external modes, NativeAOT satellite inputs are removed before the ILC response file is written.

`ExternalAll` additionally passes a content-hashed substitution file that removes the catalogued SDK-owned neutral resource tables. Hashing the copied substitution filename ensures edits invalidate incremental native compilation.

The final SDK continues to contain one managed copy of each owner/satellite family and no `dotnet-aot.resources.dll`.

## User-visible behavior

NativeAOT command help now honors `DOTNET_CLI_UI_LANGUAGE` and uses the same managed satellite strings as the managed CLI.

The retained matrix compared exit code, stdout, and stderr for:

- invariant plus all 13 shipped cultures;
- `--version`;
- root help; and
- `sln --help`.

All 126 comparisons matched the managed CLI exactly.

## Size results

Windows x64 Release NativeAOT publishes:

| Mode | Native size | Delta from Embedded | Mstat resources |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `Embedded` | 20,107,264 B | — | 97 / 3,551,857 B |
| `ExternalLocalized` | 17,324,544 B | **-2,782,720 B (-13.84%)** | 32 / 789,881 B |
| `ExternalAll` | 17,065,472 B | **-3,041,792 B (-15.13%)** | 22 / 524,359 B |

The adapted-source implementation is also 2–2.5 KB smaller than the earlier binary-backed prototype.

No `touki.dll` remains in the managed dependency graph or SDK layout. The resource runtime is part of the existing CoreUtils assembly.

## Startup results

The retained Windows x64 matrix used:

- 30 launches per mode/culture/scenario;
- balanced launch ordering;
- warm fresh-process and practical-cold states;
- invariant, French, Japanese, and Traditional Chinese cultures; and
- 2,160 measured launches after warmup.

A bounded focused rerun was retained for noisy Japanese `sln --help` cases.

| Candidate | Cases passing both 5% and 1.0 ms gates | Decision |
|---|---:|---|
| `ExternalLocalized` | **24/24** | Default |
| `ExternalAll` | 8/24 | Measurement only |

A follow-up `OptimizationPreference=Speed` experiment made every measured `sln --help` case 4.02–5.74 ms slower and grew the native images by 22–26%, so the product remains optimized for size.

## Validation

- CoreUtils resource tests: **18/18 passed**
- Resource generator tests: **56/56 passed**
- CoreUtils net472 build: **0 warnings/errors**
- Managed `dotnet-aot.Tests`: **181 passed, 15 expected skips, 0 failed**
- Native resource tests:
  - `Embedded`: **15 passed, 1 mode-specific skip**
  - `ExternalLocalized`: **16/16 passed**
  - `ExternalAll`: **16/16 passed**
- Clean managed CLI, AOT product, and AOT test builds: **0 warnings/errors**
- Clean NativeAOT publish in all three modes
- Full default Release redist build
- Real muxer AOT and managed-fallback smoke
- Flat, separated, and self-locating SDK layouts
- 126/126 functional culture/command comparisons
- Nine no-managed-fallback preflights
- PowerShell/XML parsing, Markdown links, and `git diff --check`

The full native test application retains three unrelated local managed-fallback failures because this machine reports `Access is denied` when the native `dn` test host loads `hostfxr`. The new resource scenarios pass, and managed fallback works through the real redist muxer.

Performance and native execution evidence in this change is Windows x64 only.

## Review structure

The PR is split into seven commits:

1. shared resource runtime;
2. analyzer-only resource generator;
3. managed resource-owner migration;
4. Embedded NativeAOT provider integration;
5. external NativeAOT resource modes;
6. validation/performance tooling; and
7. documentation and contributor guidance.

Issues.Body: # Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-69304 – ASP.NET Core Denial of Service Vulnerability ## Executive summary Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in ASP.NET Core IIS out-of-process hosting and request decompression. This advisory also provides guidance on what developers can do to update their applications to remove this vulnerability. The IIS Middleware for ASP.NET Core did not properly constrain decompression of certain types of request, leading to excess memory consumption and a Denial of Service. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/discussions/69155 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** Medium - **Score:** 5.9 - **Vector:** Issues.Body: # Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-69806 – .NET Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability ## Executive summary Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in .NET SDK dotnet watch. This advisory also provides guidance on what developers can do to update their applications to remove this vulnerability. The dotnet-watch AspireServerService exposes information through the use of certain arguments, that in turn can enable code injection. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/issues/56167 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 7.0 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H` - **Weakness:** CWE-200 (Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor); CWE-94 (Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection')) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** Linux - **Architectures:** All ## Affected .NET SDKs The vulnerability affects Linux installations of the .NET SDK in the version ranges listed below. These are SDK versions, not NuGet package versions. ### .NET 11 RC1 SDK feature band | Affected SDK version | Patched SDK version ---------------- | -------------------- | ------------------- 11.0.1xx RC1 | Earlier .NET 11 previews | 11.0.100-rc.1 ### .NET 10 SDK feature band | Affected SDK version | Patched SDK version ---------------- | -------------------- | ------------------- 10.0.1xx | >= 10.0.100, <= 10.0.110 | 10.0.111 10.0.3xx | >= 10.0.300, <= 10.0.399 | 10.0.400 ### .NET 9 SDK feature band | Affected SDK version | Patched SDK version ---------------- | -------------------- | ------------------- 9.0.3xx | >= 9.0.300, <= 9.0.316 | 9.0.317 ## Advisory FAQ ### How do I know if I am affected? If using an SDK listed in [affected .NET SDKs](#affected-sdks) on Linux, you're exposed to the vulnerability. ### How do I fix the issue? 1. Using the NuGet Package Manager Console in Visual Studio: - Open your project in Visual Studio. - Navigate to "Tools > NuGet Package Manager > Package Manager Console". - To update a specific package to its latest version, use the following Update-Package command: ```Update-Package -Id System.Security.Cryptography.Xml``` Using the .NET CLI (Command Line Interface): - Open a terminal or command prompt in your project's directory. - To update a specific package to its latest version, use the following add package command: ```dotnet add package System.Security.Cryptography.Xml``` Once you have updated the nuget package reference you must recompile and deploy your application. Additionally we recommend you update your runtime and/or SDKs, but it is not necessary to patch the vulnerability. ## Other Information ### Reporting Security Issues If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the [MSRC Researcher Portal](https://msrc.microsoft.com/report/vulnerability/new). Issues.Title: Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-50526 | .NET Tampering Vulnerability
Issues.Body: ## Executive summary Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in .NET SDK (Microsoft.NET.Build.Containers). This advisory also provides guidance on what developers can do to update their applications to remove this vulnerability. A tampering vulnerability exists in the .NET SDK (.NET 8, .NET 9, and .NET 10) container image build process which could allow a local attacker to inject resources that could be incorporated into container images built by other users on the same machine. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/issues/55274 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 7.0 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H` - **Weakness:** CWE-59 (Improper Link Resolution Before File Access ('Link Following')) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** All - **Architectures:** All ## Affected Packages The vulnerability affects any Microsoft .NET project if it uses any of affected package versions listed below ### .NET 10.0 Package name | Affected version | Patched version ------------ | ---------------- | ------------------------- [Microsoft.NET.Build.Containers](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.NET.Build.Containers) | >= 10.0.0, <= 10.0.9 | 10.0.10 ### .NET 9.0 Package name | Affected version | Patched version ------------ | ---------------- | ------------------------- [Microsoft.NET.Build.Containers](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.NET.Build.Containers) | >= 9.0.0, <= 9.0.17 | 9.0.18 ### .NET 8.0 Package name | Affected version | Patched version ------------ | ---------------- | ------------------------- [Microsoft.NET.Build.Containers](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.NET.Build.Containers) | >= 8.0.0, <= 8.0.28 | 8.0.29 ## Advisory FAQ ### How do I know if I am affected? If using a package listed in [affected packages](#affected-packages), you're exposed to the vulnerability. ### How do I fix the issue? 1. To fix the issue please install the latest version of .NET. If you have installed one or more .NET SDKs through Visual Studio, Visual Studio will prompt you to update Visual Studio, which will also update your .NET SDKs. 2. If your application references the vulnerable nuget package, update the package reference to the patched version. You can list the versions you have installed by running the `dotnet --info` command. * If you're using .NET 8.0, you should download and install .NET 8.0.29 Runtime or .NET 8.0.129 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/8.0. * If you're using .NET 9.0, you should download and install .NET 9.0.18 Runtime or .NET 9.0.316 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/9.0. * If you're using .NET 10.0, you should download and install .NET 10.0.10 Runtime or .NET 10.0.302 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/10.0. Once you have installed the updated runtime or SDK, restart your apps for the update to take effect. Additionally, if you've deployed [self-contained applications](https://docs.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/deploying/#self-contained-deployments-scd) targeting any of the impacted versions, these applications are also vulnerable and must be recompiled and redeployed. ## Other Information ### Reporting Security Issues If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the [MSRC Researcher Portal](https://msrc.microsoft.com/report/vulnerability/new). Further information can be found in the MSRC [Report an Issue FAQ](https://www.microsoft.com/msrc/faqs-report-an-issue). Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty. ### Support You can ask questions about this issue on GitHub in the .NET GitHub organization. The main repos are located at https://github.com/dotnet/sdk.
